To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) L-1, 2-propanediols exits from Escherichiacoli more rapidly than does L-lactaldehyde; (ii) L-1,2-propanedioloxygenation is the major pathway for catabolism of fucose under aerobic conditions; and (iii) the inner membrane of Escherichia colicells is more permeable to L-1, 2-propanediol than to L-lactaldehyde.
the C-4- to C-6-fragment of L-fucose is retained in Escherichia coil when it is oxidized to lactate but is rapidly excreted when it is reduced to 1,2-propane diol.
the C-3 fragment of fucose is retained in the cell, and the C-4 and C-6 fragments are excreted as lactaldehyde and propanediola, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a metabolic pathway that is not only of interest for its own sake but also as a model for the regulation of a pathway that is important for the catabolism of a variety of carbohydrates.

the regulation of the fate of the C-1-to-C3 fragment and the C-4 to C-6 fragment of L-fucose in the wild-type strain, as well as in isogenic mutants defective in the catabolic pathways for lactaldehyde and/or propanediol.
the metabolic fate of the C-1-to-C3 fragment of fucose, which is the major metabolic product of fucose fermentation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the fate of fucose depends on the competition of two enzymes for the same intermediate and on the permeability of the inner cell membrane.
L-lactaldehyde exits the cell much less rapidly than the corresponding 3-carbon reduction product.
propanediol exits faster than lactaldehyde because of its greater permeability through the inner membrane.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the C-1-to-C3 and C-4-to C-6 fragments of fucose are metabolized at different rates, with the former fragment being rapidly assimilated and the latter fragment being rapidly excreted.
the C-4 to C-6 fragment of L-fucose is excreted from the cell as propanediol, and not as lactaldehyde, when fucose is catabolized anaerobically.
the fate of the C-3 fragment is to exit the cell as dihydroxyacetophosphate, while that of the C-6 fragment is to exit as L-1, 2-propanediolate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the fate of lactaldehydes depends on its oxidation to lactate or its reduction to 1,2-pro-panediol.
the fate of the C-6 fragment of the hexose sugar is controlled by the redox state of the cell.
the fucose catabolism system of E. coli provides a model system in which to investigate the mechanisms of transport of small molecules.
